article_title: Are Learning Styles Relevant to Virtual Reality?
citation: Chwen Jen Chen, Seong Chong Toh, & Wan Mohd Fauzy Wan Ismail. (2005). Are Learning Styles Relevant To Virtual Reality? Journal of Research on Technology in Education, 38(2). https://www.iste.org
title: Provide VR-based learning environments with navigational aids to reduce extraneous cognitive load and improve learning outcomes
description: The article recommends designing VR learning environments with proper instructional support, specifically navigational aids such as a map tracer and directional arrows. It argues that "The eﬀorts to stay oriented when navigating through virtual environments take up mental resources" that would otherwise be available for understanding domain concepts, so aids supply the missing spatial-orientation schema and free resources for intrinsic load.
requirements: The learning problem requires learners to navigate within a virtual environment during learning
constraints: The article's evidence comes from one learning problem (beginning driver instruction) with intact classes and no pre-experimental sampling equivalence
target_learners: Form Four secondary students (approximately 16 years old) learning beginning driver instruction
target_learning_goals: Understanding of traffic rules and traffic signs in road scenarios
examples: The VR (guided exploration) mode provided "a tracer that provides a real-time indicator of the virtual vehicle position on a map, and directional arrows", and significantly outperformed the non-guided mode for both learning styles.
key_sources: Chwen Jen Chen, Seong Chong Toh, & Wan Mohd Fauzy Wan Ismail. (2005). Are Learning Styles Relevant To Virtual Reality? Journal of Research on Technology in Education, 38(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ728898

article_title: GADRRS: Guidance and Agreement for Data Harmony, Responsibility, Retention, and Sharing
citation: Lastinger Center for Learning, University of Florida. (2024). Guidance and Agreement for Data harmony, Responsibility, Retention, and Sharing (GADRRS). https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nd/4.0/
title: Tailor shared student data narrowly to what is essential for the authorized purpose
description: The agreement requires that disclosure of education records be for an education purpose and that access be narrowly tailored so that personally identifiable information is disclosed only as essential to carry out the evaluation, study, project, service, or program. It operationalizes this through checkbox exhibits listing Industry-Standard Data, Additional Data, and Excluded Data, so parties enumerate exactly which fields transfer. This gives education agencies a concrete mechanism for minimum-necessary data sharing when outsourcing services or research.
requirements: Parties must specify shared data in Exhibit D and may list excluded data; use of the data is limited to providing the Services under the agreement.
constraints: The article frames this within FERPA exceptions (Studies Exception and School Official exception); disclosure outside these exceptions is not addressed.
target_learners: K-12 students whose education records are shared
target_learning_goals: Protecting student privacy while enabling instructional improvement and authorized educational research
examples: Exhibit D Part 1 lists industry-standard fields such as names, IDs, demographics, and achievement measures, while Part 3 records data that will not be transferred.
key_sources: Lastinger Center for Learning, University of Florida. (2024). Guidance and Agreement for Data harmony, Responsibility, Retention, and Sharing (GADRRS). https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nd/4.0/

article_title: Should Schools Be Conducting Lockdown Drills?
citation: Schildkraut, J., Grogan, K., & Nabors, A. (2020). Should schools be conducting lockdown drills? WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/schools-lockdown-drills/
title: Follow NASP best practices when conducting lockdown drills: careful planning, announced drills, accommodation of vulnerable students, and debriefing
description: The brief relays the National Association of School Psychologists' guidance for conducting lockdown drills in ways that minimize psychological harm. NASP (2017) "recommends, for example, that drills be carefully planned and that a school safety team be involved in such preparations", that schools consider the needs of students with disabilities or mental health concerns, that drills "never be unannounced", and that participants be debriefed at the conclusion. The brief presents this guidance as the current best-practice standard despite the limited research base.
requirements: Drills should be carefully planned with a school safety team involved; drills should never be unannounced and participants should be debriefed.
constraints: The brief notes research on lockdown drills is sparse, so the guidance rests on expert recommendation rather than a robust evidence base.
target_learners: students with disabilities or mental health concerns
target_learning_goals: emergency preparedness
responding appropriately during a lockdown
examples: NASP's 2017 guidance recommends planning, school safety team involvement, announced drills, and debriefing; its 2018 guidance adds trauma mitigation such as providing clear information and directions and maintaining a controlled response.
key_sources: Schildkraut, J., Grogan, K., & Nabors, A. (2020). Should schools be conducting lockdown drills? WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/schools-lockdown-drills/

article_title: Educator Learning to Enact the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Flook, L., Schachner, A., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Cantor, P., & Osher, D.). (2021). Educator learning to enact the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/859.776
title: NAE framework for teacher education: three knowledge areas joined with skills and dispositions to form adaptive expertise
description: Drawing on the National Academy of Education report Preparing Teachers for a Changing World, the report describes three general areas of knowledge beginning teachers must acquire: knowledge of learners and how they learn and develop within social contexts, understanding of subject matter and curriculum in light of the social purposes of education, and understanding of teaching in light of content and learners as informed by assessment. These areas "must be joined with skills of curriculum design and instruction, inquiry, reflection, and diagnosis to produce the adaptive expertise that enables teachers to make the connections between children and content that are necessary for learning," further joined to dispositions supporting empathy, cultural competence, and equity.
requirements: Development of a vision for teaching relies on the fusion between coursework and clinical work—theory and practice
constraints: How People Learn II does not change this central conception but emphasizes sociocultural and motivational influences on learning more clearly
target_learning_goals: adaptive expertise in connecting children and content for deep learning
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., Flook, L., Schachner, A., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Cantor, P., & Osher, D.). (2021). Educator learning to enact the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/859.776

article_title: Jim Crow Debt: How Black Borrowers Experience Student Loans
citation: Mustaffa, J. B., & Davis, J. C. W. (2021). Jim Crow Debt: How Black Borrowers Experience Student Loans. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/black-student-debt-study/
title: National Black Student Loan Debt Study (survey of 1,272 Black borrowers plus 100 in-depth interviews)
description: A sequential, equal status mixed-method study of Black borrowers' experiences with student loans, conducted by The Education Trust with Jalil B. Mustaffa. "In total, 1,272 Black borrowers completed our survey," recruited via social media ads, email alerts, and word of mouth, followed by in-depth interviews with 100 volunteers selected on demographic characteristics and analyzed with the constant comparative method. The sample is largely four-year and graduate-degree holders, women, borrowers aged 25 and older, earning $50,000 or more annually.
requirements: Participants must identify as Black borrowers; survey instrument elicits perspectives on mental health, information quality, pandemic impact, return on investment, and solutions
constraints: Non-random sampling scheme; sample skews toward degree holders, women, and borrowers earning $50,000 or more annually, so findings may not generalize to all Black borrowers
target_learners: Black student loan borrowers in higher education, including graduate-degree holders and parent borrowers
target_learning_goals: Understanding Black borrowers' lived experiences of student debt to inform student loan and college affordability policy
examples: Survey data were cleaned, recoded, and analyzed using frequencies and descriptive statistics; the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Pennsylvania
key_sources: Mustaffa, J. B., & Davis, J. C. W. (2021). Jim Crow Debt: How Black Borrowers Experience Student Loans. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/black-student-debt-study/

article_title: Parent PLUS Loans Are a Double-Edged Sword for Black Borrowers
citation: Victoria Jackson, Brittani Williams, and Jalil B. Mustaffa. (2023). Parent PLUS Loans Are a Double-Edged Sword for Black Borrowers. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/parent-plus-loans-are-a-double-edged-sword-for-black-borrowers
title: National Black Student Debt Study
description: The National Black Student Debt Study is the mixed-methods research project underlying this brief and the broader #BlackStudentDebt series, led by Jalil B. Mustaffa with the Equity Research Cooperative. The brief describes it as including "a survey of nearly 1,300 Black borrowers and in-depth interviews with 100 borrowers." This brief, the fourth in a series, combines the study's qualitative data and participant quotes (under pseudonyms at participants' request) with federal data to examine Black parents' Parent PLUS borrowing.
requirements: Participants' names are replaced with pseudonyms at their request, so quotes are anonymized in publication.
constraints: The study covers Black borrowers in the United States; this brief focuses specifically on parents holding Parent PLUS loans rather than all borrower experiences.
target_learners: Black undergraduate students and their parents financing college
target_learning_goals: Understanding how financing structures shape Black families' access to and persistence in higher education
examples: The brief quotes participants such as Marcus, Noelle, Marissa, Jade, and Walter describing room-and-board shortfalls, deferment cycles, and postponed retirement.

article_title: Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of a Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education
citation: Angxuan Chen, Yuang Wei, Huixiao Le, Yan Zhang. (2024). Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15226
title: Use natural-language teaching tasks with ChatGPT agents to promote deeper cognitive processing in learning-by-teaching
description: Because teaching an agent through free natural-language dialogue produced knowledge and SRL gains, the article recommends that "educators create tasks requiring students to teach or explain concepts to ChatGPT agents using natural language to promote deeper cognitive processes". Natural dialogue stands in for the human peer that traditional learning-by-teaching requires and avoids the button-clicking and blank-filling interactions of earlier teachable agents.
requirements: A ChatGPT-based teachable agent that accepts free natural-language explanation rather than predefined response options
constraints: Supported so far only in programming education with university students in a short-term task
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of algorithms
deeper explanation and reorganization of knowledge through teaching
examples: Experimental-group participants were required to guide the ChatGPT agent using only natural language, explaining the backtracking algorithm and instructing the agent to follow their reasoning
key_sources: Angxuan Chen, Yuang Wei, Huixiao Le, Yan Zhang. (2024). Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15226

article_title: \"If You Can't Dance Your Program, You Can't Write It\": Challenges and Implications for AI in Education
citation: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education.
title: NAO humanoid robot with Choregraphe programming environment for embodied educational support
description: The article cites the humanoid robot NAO, used to support students with autism spectrum disorders, as a notable advancement transferring Embodied AI principles into education. Its programming environment Choregraphe "relies on visual blocks and Python code, facilitates the creation of integrated multimodal behaviors (voice, vision, touch, movement)", yet the article reports it "still lacks flexibility in unpredictable scenarios", with improvisational and adaptive operation remaining in early stages.
requirements: Open environments sensitive to situational emergence, which the article says remain underdeveloped
constraints: The system's ability to operate improvisationally or adaptively remains in its early stages, reflecting a structural gap in development
target_learning_goals: embodied, multimodal learning support integrating voice, vision, touch, and movement
examples: The article describes Choregraphe as enabling creation of integrated multimodal behaviors combining voice, vision, touch, and movement.

article_title: A meta-analysis of morphological interventions: effects on literacy achievement of children with literacy difficulties
citation: U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics. (2007). Reading 2007: National Assessment of Educational Progress at Grades 4 and 8. NCES 2007–496. https://nationsreportcard.gov
title: NAEP reading framework: reading performance measured in two dimensions — three contexts for reading and four aspects of reading
description: The NAEP reading framework is the blueprint specifying what the reading assessment measures. It defines reading broadly as developing a general understanding of texts, interpreting texts, and using texts for different purposes, and views reading as "an interactive and dynamic process involving the reader, the text, and the context of the reading experience." It specifies two dimensions: three contexts for reading (literary experience, information, performing a task) guiding text selection, and four aspects of reading guiding question types. The framework has guided the assessment since 1992 with updates that did not change content, permitting trend comparisons.
requirements: Assessment time is distributed across the aspects of reading per framework targets (e.g., 60% at grade 4 for general understanding/developing interpretation combined)
constraints: All three contexts are assessed at grade 8 but only two at grade 4
Scales are set separately for each context, so direct comparisons cannot be made from one context to another
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension across literary experience, information, and task-performance contexts
examples: The 2007 fourth-grade assessment included 10 reading passages and 100 questions divided between reading for literary experience and reading for information
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics. (2007). Reading 2007: National Assessment of Educational Progress at Grades 4 and 8. NCES 2007–496. https://nationsreportcard.gov

article_title: A meta-analysis of morphological interventions: effects on literacy achievement of children with literacy difficulties
citation: U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics. (2007). Reading 2007: National Assessment of Educational Progress at Grades 4 and 8. NCES 2007–496. https://nationsreportcard.gov
title: NAEP reading assessment design: matrix sampling of passages, achievement levels, and item maps for interpreting scale scores
description: The 2007 NAEP reading assessment is a nationally representative measure in which "each student took just a portion of the test, consisting of two 25-minute sections or one 50-minute section," with multiple-choice and constructed-response questions. Results are reported on a 0–500 scale, as percentages at or above Basic, Proficient, and Advanced achievement levels, and via item maps showing what students at different scale points can do. In 2007 more than 350,000 students at grades 4 and 8 participated, including 191,000 fourth-graders in 7,830 schools.
requirements: Testing accommodations for students with disabilities and English language learners, introduced in 1998, to allow fair participation
constraints: A portion of students remains excluded even with accommodations; variation in exclusion and accommodation rates should be considered when comparing performance over time and across states
Achievement levels are used on a trial basis and should be interpreted with caution
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension measurement and progress monitoring
examples: An item map shows fourth-graders near the middle of the Basic range (average score 220) were likely to recognize the meaning of specialized vocabulary from context
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics. (2007). Reading 2007: National Assessment of Educational Progress at Grades 4 and 8. NCES 2007–496. https://nationsreportcard.gov

article_title: Working memory development from early childhood to adolescence using two nationally representative samples.
citation: Ahmed, S. F., Ellis, A., Ward, K. P., Chaku, N., & Davis-Kean, P. E. (2022). Working memory development from early childhood to adolescence using two nationally representative samples. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001396
title: Use national developmental trends of working memory as a reference for interpreting individual studies and timing interventions
description: The article argues that population-level WM growth charts serve as a normative reference, "akin to national height or weight standards in medical settings", allowing researchers to interpret intervention effects independent of age-related change and helping clinicians and educators identify periods of rapid WM growth. The study supplies such trends from ages 3–19 using two nationally representative samples.
requirements: Nationally representative longitudinal data with repeated WM measures across a wide age range
constraints: Findings are verbal WM only and generalizable to the U.S. population, which the authors note is only a small fraction of the human population
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting the development of working memory relevant to learning, reasoning, and problem solving
examples: The authors charted forward and backward digit span from ages 3–19 in the PSID-CDS and numbers reversed across nine waves in the ECLS-K:2011, publishing predicted means by age and wave.
key_sources: Ahmed, S. F., Ellis, A., Ward, K. P., Chaku, N., & Davis-Kean, P. E. (2022). Working memory development from early childhood to adolescence using two nationally representative samples. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001396

article_title: Dyscalculia in Early Adulthood: Implications for Numerical Activities of Daily Living
citation: Vigna Giulia, Ghidoni Enrico, Burgio Francesca, Danesin Laura, Angelini Damiano, Benavides-Varela Silvia, Semenza Carlo. (2022). Dyscalculia in Early Adulthood: Implications for Numerical Activities of Daily Living. Brain Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/brainsci12030373
title: NADL (Numerical Activities of Daily Living) standardized battery
description: The NADL is a standardized test created "to identify impairments in numerical functions that may cause problems in day-to-day and ecologically valid tasks". It comprises a Participant Interview assessing awareness of numerical abilities, an Informal Test of everyday numerical activities (time, measure, distance, communication, general knowledge, money), and a Formal Test of school-acquired skills (number comprehension, transcoding, mental and written calculation, rules and principles). Maximum scores are 10, 23, and 77 respectively; the original standardization reports Cronbach's alpha = 0.73. In this study it was administered to adults with DD for the first time, as experimental tasks compared against a control group rather than as a diagnostic tool.
requirements: Administered with orally provided instructions and answers in the Interview and Informal sections, requiring no reading of texts
constraints: In this study the NADL subtests were not used as diagnostic tools but as experimental hypothesis-driven tasks compared against a control group rather than normative data
target_learners: adults with neurological or numerical impairments
target_learning_goals: assessment of formal and everyday numerical skills
awareness of numerical abilities
examples: Administered to 26 adults with DD and 26 healthy controls, with the Interview and Informal sections delivered orally
key_sources: Vigna Giulia, Ghidoni Enrico, Burgio Francesca, Danesin Laura, Angelini Damiano, Benavides-Varela Silvia, Semenza Carlo. (2022). Dyscalculia in Early Adulthood: Implications for Numerical Activities of Daily Living. Brain Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/brainsci12030373

article_title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y
title: Natural information processing system: five principles underlying cognitive load theory
description: The article grounds cognitive load theory in an architecture in which biologically secondary knowledge processing is analogous to evolution by natural selection, described by five principles: information store, borrowing and reorganising, randomness as genesis, narrow limits of change, and environmental organising and linking. Long-term memory provides the store; working memory is severely limited for novel information but has no known limits for organised information retrieved from long-term memory. The authors state these systems 'can be described using five principles summarised in Table 1'.
requirements: Novel information must be processed by a working memory limited in capacity and duration, while information retrieved from long-term memory is unconstrained
constraints: The limits of change principle applies only to novel information, not familiar information retrieved from long-term memory
target_learning_goals: acquisition of domain-specific knowledge and skills in long-term memory
examples: Table 1 lists the five principles and their functions, e.g. the information store principle: 'Store information in long-term memory for indefinite periods'

article_title: Show me your opinion. Perceptual cues in creating and reading argument diagrams
citation: Marije van Amelsvoort, Alfons Maes. (2016). Show me your opinion. Perceptual cues in creating and reading argument diagrams. Instructional Science 44:335–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9378-9
title: Natural cognitive resources framework: primary metaphors, Gestalt principles and cultural conventions as sources of perceptual cues in argument diagrams
description: The article frames the production and interpretation of argument-diagram perceptual cues as drawing on three "'natural' and partially overlapping cognitive resources": embodied experiences yielding metaphoric conceptualizations (primary metaphors), general visual preferences (Gestalt theory), and cultural conventions such as reading direction and color symbolism. Perceptual cues are categorized as spatial, graphical and textual elements following design guidelines on visual variables. The framework organized the coding of both studies and, in the authors' view, "enables us to shed light on what lay-people do when asked to spontaneously create a for or against argument diagram."
requirements: Learners must be untrained in formal argument-diagram conventions for the natural-resource predictions to apply; trained conventions will change visualization preferences and practices, as the article states
constraints: The framework was studied for for-against argument diagrams with simple predefined argumentative information, not complex layered argument structures or collaborative construction of a debate space
target_learners: untrained lay-people and students creating or reading argument diagrams
target_learning_goals: expressing and interpreting argumentative position in argument diagrams
structuring argumentation visually for communication and decision-making
examples: Twenty students drew for-against diagrams on a whiteboard from argument cards; their use of space, boxes, lines, arrows, color and text was coded against the framework's expectations
key_sources: Marije van Amelsvoort, Alfons Maes. (2016). Show me your opinion. Perceptual cues in creating and reading argument diagrams. Instructional Science 44:335–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9378-9

article_title: Testing the use of variation theory in teaching critical thinking—a field experimental study
citation: Kristoffer Larsson · Klas Andersson. (2025). Testing the use of variation theory in teaching critical thinking—a field experimental study. Instructional Science (2025) 53:1025–1046. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09721-y
title: Intervention teaching material: national-test tasks and scored student responses from a national database operationalizing contrast and generalization
description: The treatment material consisted of "the three tasks, i.e. the voting-age task, the referendum task and the wage-difference task, and student responses to these three tasks taken from the database" — a nationwide sample of about 600 complete Swedish national test responses per year. Student responses were pre-analysed and sorted into those showing zero to three alternations of points of view, enabling teachers to vary the aspect (number of alternations) against an invariant task for contrast, and vary tasks against an invariant value for generalization. Control teachers worked the same tasks without access to the database responses.
requirements: Access to scored student responses illustrating graded values of the target aspect, obtained from analysis of a national test database
constraints: Control teachers had no access to the student responses from the database, so the two conditions differed in materials as well as method
target_learners: Swedish 9th grade students in social studies
target_learning_goals: Alternating points of view on societal issues such as voting age, referendums and wage differences
examples: Four voting-age responses (Table 1) illustrated zero, one, two and three alternations of points of view and were used in the contrast pattern.

article_title: Examining Black and Latine Students’ Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review
citation: Harris-Thomas, B., Nicolai, K. D., Chen, X.-Y., & Areizaga Barbieri, C. (2026). Examining Black and Latine Students' Sense of Belonging within the Mathematics Classroom: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10181-0
title: Reviewed corpus of 20 studies on Black and Latine adolescents' mathematics belonging
description: The review's evidence base comprises 20 manuscripts: 14 identified through systematic search methods (five databases, ancestry search, grey literature request, Covidence screening) plus 13 added during the narrative review phase via backward snowballing. Studies span quantitative surveys (e.g., 2,938 Algebra I students in Morales-Chicas & Graham, 2021), qualitative interviews, focus groups, observations, and video data. Each study was coded for data sources, sample characteristics, belonging or related constructs, and approach to race/ethnicity using DeCuir-Gunby and Schutz's classification.
requirements: Included studies reported results or findings specifically for Black and/or Latine students, focused on adolescents in U.S. school mathematics settings, and named belonging or a closely related construct
constraints: The review transitioned from systematic to narrative review methods, expanding inclusion criteria and weighting studies unequally based on the authors' expertise
target_learners: Black and Latine adolescent mathematics students in U.S. middle and high schools
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting sense of belonging and related constructs (math identity, connectedness, engagement) in mathematics classrooms
examples: Table 2 snapshots each study, e.g., Maloney and Matthews (2020) with 12 teachers and 321 Black and Latine students, and Gray et al. (2024) with 255 sixth-grade students

article_title: The use of a composition scale.
citation: Truman L. Kelley; Ernest C. Witham. (1918). Communications and Discussions. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Nassau Supplement: a composition rating scale scored in steps 0–9, used alongside percentage ratings
description: The Nassau Supplement is a scale for rating the quality of written compositions, scored in steps from 0 to 9. In Witham's account, students first rated a composition "on the percentage basis" and, the following day, "rated the same composition by the Nassau Supplement", yielding frequency distributions across the ten scale steps that were compared with the ten percentage groups.
requirements: Raters must study the scale before applying it, as Witham's students did after a further study of the scale
target_learners: normal-school students learning tests and measurements
seventh-grade pupils whose compositions are rated
target_learning_goals: reliable evaluation of written composition quality
examples: A mixed class on Tests and Measurements of 16 students in a summer normal school rated a typewritten composition first on the percentage basis and then by the Nassau Supplement

article_title: Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience
citation: Robert Colvin. (2016). Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.12
title: Direct neuroscience input to broad education policy matters is unlikely; focus narrowly on cognitive-level optimisation, generalisation and integration
description: The article recommends a narrow focus: neuroscience is unlikely to directly impact aspects of education such as teacher career paths, governmental policy or curriculum. Its greatest impact comes when it builds upon existing education research into effective learning and addresses the right questions, namely optimising, generalising and integrating existing interventions at the cognitive level. Interventions must remain sensitive to the social and cultural aspects of a particular learning environment.
requirements: Research must build on the existing wealth of education research into effective learning
The right questions must be addressed, at the cognitive level
constraints: Neuroscience is unlikely to directly impact teacher career paths, governmental policy or curriculum
Interventions must be sensitive to social and cultural aspects of the particular learning environment
Considerations such as class size must be balanced against financial and administrative realities
target_learning_goals: increasing the scope and benefit of effective instructional interventions
examples: The article points to Hattie's synthesis of techniques that influence learning as an ideal starting place for deeper research into effective teaching interventions
key_sources: Robert Colvin. (2016). Optimising, generalising and integrating educational practice using neuroscience. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.12

article_title: When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear
citation: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4
title: Observe behavior in naturalistic conditions before adopting tightly controlled laboratory paradigms for studying a brain system
description: The article's methodological lesson: a research community "can be biased by relying on an attractive, controlled laboratory paradigm". When a rat faces one threatening stimulus allowing a single reflexive response, one is bound to find neuronal responses tightly linked to the CS. Only when the situation allows behavioral flexibility can one examine the relation between stimuli, neuronal activity, decisions and responses. It echoes O'Keefe and Nadel's recommendation that "observational studies in naturalistic conditions should be performed prior to using controlled laboratory paradigms".
requirements: Experimental situations that allow behavioral flexibility, and parallel measurements of autonomic responses such as pupil dilation, gastric motility, heart and respiration rate
constraints: Naturalistic tasks are harder to interpret: movement-related correlates may or may not reflect decision processes about food and threats, unlike the simpler study of tone-evoked activity followed by reflexive freezing, per the article
target_learners: researchers designing studies of neural systems underlying learning and behavior
target_learning_goals: choosing research paradigms that reveal what neurons code for across a large behavioral repertoire
examples: The article contrasts fear conditioning's single reflexive response with foraging and platform-mediated avoidance tasks where animals express avoidance, feeding and hesitation
key_sources: Paré, D. & Quirk, G. J. (2017). When scientific paradigms lead to tunnel vision: lessons from the study of fear. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0007-4

article_title: Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance
citation: Alvarez, N., Sanchez-Ruiz, A., Cavazza, M., Shigematsu, M., & Prendinger, H. (2014). Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25, 35–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0022-z
title: Narrative Balance Management: drama management via Balance, Global Balance, Impact and Intensity parameters
description: The Narrative Balance Management account models a training session's dramatic flow with four parameters adapted from dimensions of conflict: Balance (how good or bad an event is for the user), Impact (its dramatic load), and the dynamic Global Balance and Intensity maintained by the system. When invoked, the manager "selects an event from the Task Trees which maximizes Impact, with the current Intensity as the upper boundary, and with the Balance most similar to the current Global Balance, but with opposite value". Global Balance attenuates toward zero over time, and empty events from a timer (set to 15 s in the system) raise Intensity so that difficulty escalates when the user is comfortable and assistance appears when the user struggles.
requirements: A domain expert must assign static Balance and Impact values to each event node when designing the scenario's task trees
A Task Model Database for the domain must be defined so the manager can be assembled into other training systems
constraints: The article notes Balance and Impact values are static and quite subjective, since they depend on expert judgment of dramatic quality
target_learners: Medical students training biohazard laboratory procedures
target_learning_goals: Biohazard spill-cleaning protocols
Handling unexpected laboratory accidents
examples: In the sample session, the manager selected a spill overflow when Intensity reached 5, and triggered a new broken-bottle spill when a fast user bumped a table
key_sources: Alvarez, N., Sanchez-Ruiz, A., Cavazza, M., Shigematsu, M., & Prendinger, H. (2014). Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25, 35–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0022-z

description: The NAEP 2023 Automatic Math Scoring Challenge provided a training dataset of 251,370 responses from 10 items (five grade 4, five grade 8) and a test dataset of 27,930 responses with withheld scores. Items required short or extended constructed responses with maximum scores between 2 and 5. The competition goal was to predict scores within QWK 0.05 of human inter-rater reliability without demographic bias (pairwise SMD > 0.10).

constraints: The dataset is not publicly available

examples: The ten items spanned algebraic representations, patterns and functions, mathematical reasoning, probability, geometry, properties of numbers, and number operations.

title: Require students to name diagram components using words or phrases from the problem text
description: In KERMIT, when a student creates a new diagram component, its name must be a word or phrase from the problem text. The authors defend this naming policy as beneficial for learning: it mirrors how students underline words in requirements, lets colour-coding show how much of the problem text is covered, aligns with Software Engineering's encouragement of "the use of the customer's language", prevents uninterpretable invented labels, and makes interpretation of students' solutions easier while avoiding natural language understanding problems.

constraints: Some have criticized the decision as being overly restrictive

examples: Using different colours for different component types makes it easier for the student to see how much of the problem text is already covered and what is still outstanding

article_title: Designing Game-Based Learning for High School Artificial Intelligence Education
citation: Leitner, M., Greenwald, E., Wang, N., Montgomery, R., & Merchant, C. (2023). Designing Game-Based Learning for High School Artificial Intelligence Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 33, 384–398. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00327-w
title: Integrate narrative, educational content, and gameplay tightly and calibrate narrative complexity to align engagement with learning in educational games
description: Drawing on the success of Crystal Island, the article adopts the principle that "tight integration between educational content, narrative, and gameplay, along with properly calibrated narrative complexity are two factors that can lead to a positive relationship between learning and engagement." ARIN-561 builds its narrative around tasks commonly solved by search algorithms (pathfinding, puzzle solving, password cracking), so students only advance the story through gameplay that teaches search algorithms. The narrative uses a straightforward escape-the-planet premise with embedded mystery to spark curiosity without distracting from learning.
requirements: narrative detailed enough to motivate problem solving but not so complex it distracts from learning
target_learning_goals: engagement with AI problem-solving tasks
examples: the game develops a companionship between the student and the robot NPC Tachi through dialogue, so engagement with the character drives problem solving

article_title: NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods
citation: Christopher Nikulin, Gabriela Lopez, Eduardo Piñonez, Luis Gonzalez, Pia Zapata. (2019). NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09657-4
title: NASA-TLX multidimensional workload questionnaire used as a common measurement instrument across design activities
description: NASA-TLX is a multi-dimensional rating procedure that assigns a total workload score based on a weighted average of six sub-scales: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort, and frustration level. Its application has two sequential phases: weighing, consisting of 15 binary comparisons among the six dimensions after task execution, and estimation, in which the individual rates each dimension on a scale from 0 to 100 immediately after task completion. In this study it was adopted as an outcome evaluation instrument for comparing different design phases and activities, with 133 questionnaires delivered.
requirements: Tasks must be represented as specific measurable activities so the questionnaire can be framed per module activity
constraints: The workload index is not an intrinsic feature of the task but results from interaction among task requirements, circumstances, capacities, and individual perceptions and behaviors
target_learning_goals: monitoring and comparing designer workload across design process activities
examples: Questionnaires were administered in Spanish at the end of each module, three per module framed for each activity, yielding 133 questionnaires across 11 modules

article_title: Battling bias: Effects of training and training context
citation: Poos, J., van den Bosch, K. & Janssen, C.P. (2017). Battling bias: Effects of training and training context. Computers & Education, vol. 111, pp. 101-113. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.04.004
title: Use engaging narrative text rather than expensive immersive games for bias-mitigation training when resources are scarce
description: This principle holds that when training content is held equal, a well-written narrative text can achieve bias-mitigation training outcomes comparable to an interactive game. The article found that "embedding training in the context of a game provides no additional performance bene ﬁts" compared with text-based narratives, and that equal immersion scores suggest "a narrative is suf ﬁcient to engage students in immersive learning". For organizations with scarce resources, the authors recommend dedicating resources to other aspects of training success rather than to a potentially expensive game.
requirements: The training content and narrative must be identical or comparable across media for the text alternative to be considered equivalent
The narrative must be engaging, as narrative has been found to increase learning and engagement
constraints: The article's evidence covers two specific biases (the fundamental attribution error and confirmation bias) and a single detective-game context
The authors state more research is needed to understand what aspects of a learning environment provide the best context for bias-mitigation training
target_learners: Adult learners in professional bias-mitigation training, such as the student and recruited adult participants in this study
target_learning_goals: Reducing cognitive biases in judgment and decision making through critical-reflective thinking
examples: Participants read text scripts of the same murder-case narratives as the game group, and trained and untrained text groups performed equivalently to their game counterparts on in-context and out-context bias measures

examples: Two separate studies were conducted to investigate the link between feedback nature, receiver evaluation, and use for product revision across educational contexts and tools.

citation: Xiang Yue, Shi Haoning, Ren Keke, Yang Xilin, Li Lin, Zhao Qinghua, Huang Huanhuan. (2026). An artificial intelligence application framework for nursing education: a scoping review based on the KAS model. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09209-4
title: Named nursing AI frameworks: N.U.R.S.E.S., AI-ABCs, and CARE
description: The review identifies existing nursing-specific AI frameworks: the N.U.R.S.E.S. framework by Hoelscher and Pugh, which "emphasizes nurses’ roles as AI collaborators"; the AI-ABCs framework by Kobeissi et al., which clarifies fundamental educational objectives; and the CARE framework by Bester and Zeigler, which "structures prompt engineering proficiency through context, action, role, and expectation elements." requirements: Frameworks must offer clear pathways for pedagogical implementation and comprehensive instructional content and assessment methodologies to translate into curricula
constraints: The review states these frameworks either lack clear implementation pathways or focus on isolated skills rather than holistic curricula

examples: The CARE framework structures prompt engineering proficiency through context, action, role, and expectation elements

title: Narrative medicine as an educational approach using narrative to understand patient illness experience
description: Narrative medicine is defined in the article as "an approach to the use of narrative to collect and interpret information on the patient's experience of illness", encouraging physicians to focus on patients' real feelings rather than laboratory and imaging results. In medical education it is integrated "through a combination of reading, reflection, storytelling and writing exercises". The review evaluates this approach against lecture-based learning across residency specialties.

humanistic care ability
doctor-patient communication skills
procedural skills

article_title: Content and outcomes of narrative medicine programmes: a systematic review of the literature through 2019.
citation: Remein Christy DiFrances C, Childs E, Pasco JC, Trinquart L, Flynn DB, Wingerter SL, Bhasin RM, Demers LB, Benjamin EJ. (2020). Content and outcomes of narrative medicine programmes: a systematic review of the literature through 2019. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-031568
title: Narrative medicine as a framework grounded in narrative competence for humane and effective medical practice
description: Narrative medicine (NM) is a framework for medicine and health sciences that values individuals' stories and experiences as integral to the lived experience of health and illness. The review attributes its foundational account to Rita Charon, who introduced the term in 2001 and asserted that "The effective practice of medicine requires narrative competence, that is, the ability to acknowledge, absorb, interpret, and act on the stories and plights of others." NM programmes operationalise this framework through close reading of published literature and creative/reflective writing, combined with group discussion and workshopping, aiming to cultivate narrative and clinical competencies.
requirements: Eligible NM training in the review had to include both essential components: textual analysis/close reading of published literature and creative/reflective writing embedded in the programmatic core.
constraints: The review notes the stated definition of NM was inconsistent even within publications meeting inclusion criteria, and its vocabulary reflects a particularly American viewpoint on academic health sciences education.
target_learners: medical, dental and health sciences students
target_learning_goals: narrative competence
empathy
reflection
relationship-building
professional identity formation
examples: Programmes in the review implemented the framework through reading published narratives and reflective writing (100% of programmes), group discussion (83.6%), sharing/workshopping writing (52.7%) and other narrative-based exercises such as patient interviews and portfolios.

article_title: Immersive Planetarium Visualizations for Teaching Solar System Moon Concepts to Undergraduates
citation: Yu, K. C., Sahami, K., Denn, G., Sahami, V., & Sessions, L. C. (2016). Immersive Planetarium Visualizations for Teaching Solar System Moon Concepts to Undergraduates. Journal of Astronomy & Earth Sciences Education, 3(2). https://www.thecluteinstitute.com
title: Narrative journey model of fulldome presentation
description: A presentation model for fulldome theaters in which "audiences are taken on virtual tours with few cuts or edits, making the visual experience nearly seamless." Point-of-view camera shots make viewers feel they are moving through space rather than observing passively, and camera motions are slowed because fast movement causes motion sickness, while cuts must be spaced so viewers can adjust to each new scene. The continuous journey across multiple scales lets viewers reflect on size relationships and link processes at different scales. The study's virtual flights through planetary moon systems were designed in this format, with one exception (camera cuts to show orbital resonance).
requirements: Interactive real-time planetarium software capable of seamless, continuous trans-scalar flightpaths between celestial bodies
A live presenter or navigator controlling the visualization in real time
constraints: Camera motions must be slowed and cuts limited to avoid motion sickness and disorientation
The study's resonance demonstration was the only exception to the continuous journey model, requiring camera cuts
target_learning_goals: understanding the number, appearance, orbital motions, and origins of moons in the Solar System
examples: The study's lecture used a seamless narrative journey tour from Earth's Moon through Mercury, Venus, Mars, and the outer planets, with no edits or cuts except the Galilean orbital resonance demonstration

title: Natural pedagogy theory: human infants are uniquely adapted to interpret ostensive-communicative cues as informative
description: Natural pedagogy theory holds that human infants possess a species-specific adaptation to interpret ostensive-communicative cues as conveying relevant, generalizable information about a specific object or location, rather than merely eliciting attention. The article uses this theory to explain why scaffolding improves children's executive function: infants expect such cues to be informative, whereas dogs treat them as imperative. The study's null result in dogs is presented as support for this account over simple attentional explanations.
requirements: Interpreting ostensive cues as informative requires an expectation that cues provide relevant and generalizable information
constraints: The theory applies to humans; dogs appear to interpret ostensive cues as requests or commands rather than information
